title: Joining the Hummingbird band after Earl Stockmeyer
summary: He befriended the five-piece house band, played Stockmeyer's banjo with uke tuning, and when Stockmeyer died Professor Cook gave him the job.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What kind of a band was that?

Well, there was a five-piece band. There was a band that was Kid Clayton on trumpet, George Williams on drum, Tink Batiste on piano, Pete Beatty playing saxophone, and Earl Stockmeyer playing banjo. So after I went there that first night and I saw that, to me, that was a new world. I felt like somebody who got rejuvenated all over again. I knew that was the life for me, that and no other life. So I began to hang in the place every night. I practically lived in it. So I got to become friends with the band. I'd bring them drinks when I'd be at the table. And Earl Stockmeyer and I got to be good friends. So when I took his banjo and I couldn't play a tenor the way a banjo should be played, but I kept fooling with it and I tuned it like I had tuned my uke. I could play that uke very well. I didn't know I could play in the band with it like that. They wasn't playing but in two keys all night, no how, B flat and F. So finally I got to know that I could play my uke. with what they were playing. And that's all I wanted to know. From that I was more understanding than Earl was. So what happens is he, about, that went on for about five or six months and one night he got very sick. And he didn't come back in the wake and about two or three weeks he died. So Professor Cook put me in the band. Says I want Creole George to stay in the band. Professor Cook was the guy who owned the joint. Him and his wife Evelyn, there was one of the finest dance teams in the city. Why did they call him Professor? Well that's what you, well you know he was just a guy was all full of flesh, always a tuxedo and a whistle in his mouth. Oh he had a big mind, you know, but he had a wonderful dance team. But he was in charge of it. And all them guys used to come around and say, Well man, you could have given the job to this banjo player and that banjo player. He said, I'm going to give it to him. He said, because I got faith in him that in six months he's going to cut everybody in town. I said, well I'm going to try to live up to it as much as I could. So I mean I was just playing, I wasn't getting nowhere, but to go back like I told you I met my cousin Margaret. And she asked me to take her to a dance one night and I heard John Moreira play. That was the banjo master. I never heard nobody in my life play no banjo like that. That was the, oh that, that, that, that, that. Words will never express how well this man could play.
